description: My name is Carter Meiners from Blinn. If you are from blinn brenham join this team
summary: We developed an application that, given a multitude of variables analyzed on the lunar surface and defining some on the spacecraft itself, calculates the most efficient positions on the moon. For those who are unaware of specific details for an analysis, a default is given for the spacecraft, so anyone can start using the site immediately, along with giving creative freedom to those well knowledged in the subject. Along with this, being able to visualize optimal landing spots and giving statistics based on your preference completes the objectives, such as changing the dates and times, analyzing the position of the Sun and the Earth, an easily accessible interface for any user regardless of technical skills, communication, and power consideration. This project is important, as we are seeing an influx of lunar exploration efforts in modern day science, and the optimization of landing sites for any sort of vessel built for space will not only save money for the giants of the industry, but also give small aerospace system startups the same freedom and accessibility.
details:
Our project is a landing site planner for the south pole of the Moon. You pick a spot near the pole and a date range, and it tells you two things: when that spot gets sunlight, and when it can see Earth. Sunlight matters because that's how a lander or rover gets power and stays warm. Seeing Earth matters because if Earth is below the horizon you can't talk to it directly, so you're stuck waiting or using a relay satellite.

We picked the south pole because that's where Artemis is going, and it's a really weird place to land. The Sun never gets more than about 1.5 degrees above the horizon there. Earth stays within about 7 degrees of the horizon and moves up and down over the month. So basically everything is skimming the ground, and one hill or crater rim 10 km away can block the Sun or Earth completely. Two spots that are close to each other can end up with really different results. We wanted a tool where you could just click around and see that for yourself instead of reading a paper about it.

The app is made in Streamlit and has three pages plus a sidebar.

The first page is a 3D Moon you can spin around and zoom into. It's shaded by sunlight (or by Earth visibility if you switch it in settings), so when you move the time slider you can watch the lit side move across the pole. There's a yellow dot for the point right under the Sun and a blue dot for the point right under Earth. We also put white dots on some known sites like the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache, Shackleton's floor, Haworth, Malapert, Cabeus, Nobile and Mons Mouton. Around the pole there's a grid of small dots and you can click any of them to pick that spot.

The second page is a flat map looking straight down at the south pole. You can color it by Sun height or Earth height and change how far out the map goes (80 to 88 degrees south). Clicking a square selects that location, same as the globe.

The third page is an About page that explains the problem, how to use the app, how the math works and what the limits are.

The sidebar is where the actual answers are. It shows whether the spot you picked is sunlit or dark right now and whether Earth is in view or blocked. It also gives the Sun's height, how much of the Sun's disk is showing, and where Earth is in the sky. Then for the whole time window it gives the percent of time with sunlight, the longest stretch of darkness in hours, the percent of time Earth is visible, the longest time without contact, and how often you get both at once. Under that there's a color bar across the whole window (yellow is Sun only, blue is Earth only, green is both, black is neither), and a 360 degree horizon view that shows the horizon around you with the paths the Sun and Earth take through the sky.

For the math, there are two files that do the real work.

ephem.py figures out where the Sun and Earth are from the Moon. We use a Python library called astronomy-engine to get the Sun and Moon positions, then turn those into directions from the Moon. Then we rotate them using the IAU model for how the Moon is tilted and spinning, so they line up with the Moon's surface. After that, for any spot, we work out which way is up, north and east and convert to azimuth (compass direction) and elevation (height above the horizon). One thing we found out is that you have to measure from the actual spot on the surface and not the center of the Moon. Earth is close enough that this changes where it appears by around a quarter of a degree, which sounds tiny but when Earth is only a couple degrees up it can be the difference between visible and blocked. We also count the Sun as a disk instead of a point, so a spot only counts as sunlit if at least half of the Sun is above the horizon.

terrain.py handles the actual ground. If you just treat the Moon as a perfect ball the results at the pole are pretty wrong, because the pole is full of big craters and ridges. So you can load a height map (DEM) from NASA's LOLA data, which is the laser altimeter on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The code shoots out lines in 360 directions from your spot, up to 150 km, checks how high the ground is along each line, subtracts for the Moon curving away, and keeps the highest angle it finds. That gives you the real horizon for that spot. Then instead of asking "is the Sun above 0 degrees" it asks "is the Sun above the mountains in that direction." If you don't load a DEM it falls back to the smooth Moon, but it still accounts for the panel or antenna being raised a bit off the ground.

What benefits does it have?

The main one is speed. Normally checking lighting for a site means writing scripts, downloading big data files and running stuff for a while. With this you click a spot and get numbers right away.

It also looks at power and communication together. A lot of what we found online only looks at sunlight, but for a real mission both matter, and the best times are when you have both. That's why we added the "Sun + Earth together" number and the color bar.

We tried to pick numbers that actually help with design. Percent sunlit is nice but the longest dark period is what tells you how big your battery has to be and how long you need heaters running. Longest comms gap tells you how long a crew or rover would be on its own.

There's also a height setting for the solar panel or antenna, from 0 to 20 m. At the pole even a few meters can change how much Sun or Earth you see, so you can test whether putting something on a mast is worth it.

You can also set any start date and a window up to a year long, so it works for "where do we land" and "when do we land."

And it's free and simple to run. It's all Python, it runs in the browser, and it doesn't need a strong computer. Install the requirements, run one command and it opens.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to actually understand why the south pole is so hard and why some spots are worth so much more than others. This could be someone doing early planning, a student learning about orbits, a teacher explaining why the poles are different from the rest of the Moon, or just someone following Artemis who wants to see what the astronauts will deal with. If someone can click on a ridge and see it gets sunlight 80 percent of the time, then click the crater next to it and see it gets basically none, that explains it better than a paragraph does.

We also hope it gets more people interested in NASA data. Everything in the project comes from public data and free libraries, so anyone can check it or build on it.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Everything is written in Python. The website part is Streamlit, which let us make the pages, sidebar and sliders without writing HTML. All the charts (the 3D globe, polar map, timeline and horizon view) are made with Plotly. NumPy does all the math, like the rotation matrices and computing angles for a whole grid of points at once. Pandas is in there for tables. astronomy-engine gives us the Sun and Moon positions and the Moon's rotation, and we picked it because it doesn't need you to download huge ephemeris files like SPICE does. rasterio reads the LOLA elevation files (GeoTIFF) and converts between latitude/longitude and map coordinates.

The data comes from NASA's LRO LOLA south pole elevation maps, which you can download from NASA Goddard's PGDA site.

No special hardware. We built and ran it on normal laptops. We used Git and GitHub to share code, and for at least one of us this project was also the first time using git.

How is your project creative?

We think the horizon view is the most creative part. It's basically what you would see if you stood on that spot and turned in a circle: the bumpy horizon, the Sun sliding along just above or below it, and Earth doing its own small loop. It turns a bunch of angles into a picture that makes sense right away.

Being able to switch between the smooth Moon and real terrain is also useful, because you can see how much the mountains change the answer. Sometimes it's a big difference.

We also wanted it to feel like exploring and not like filling out a form. You can type coordinates if you want, but you can also spin the globe and click on stuff.

And we tried to get the small details right (measuring from the surface, the size of the Sun, panel height, curvature) while keeping the app simple enough that you don't need to know any of that to use it.

What factors did your team consider?

Accuracy was the big one. Near the pole a small error can flip the answer from lit to dark, so we spent a lot of time on the geometry details mentioned above.

Speed was another. Recomputing everything every time you moved a slider was way too slow, so we cache the Sun/Earth positions, the elevation map and the horizon for each spot. The terrain code samples close distances finely and far distances more spread out, and it does all 360 directions at once with NumPy instead of a loop.

We also had to make clicking work. Streamlit doesn't send back the data we attached to the point you clicked, only which chart layer and which point number, so we had to keep our own lookup table to turn a click back into a latitude and longitude. We also had to stop the same click from triggering over and over when the page reloads.

We thought about who would use it. Engineers want numbers and students want something they can play with, so we have the globe for exploring, the sidebar for numbers, and the About page explaining it in plain words.

We also wanted to be upfront about the limits. The smooth Moon option warns you that it ignores mountains and craters, and the sidebar always says which horizon you're using. Right now the reference site coordinates are approximate and still need to be swapped for the exact ones from NASA's Artemis III maps. The globe and map shading always use the smooth Moon (only the sidebar uses terrain), and Earth visibility doesn't take into account things like ground station schedules or which way an antenna can point. Next we want to fix the site coordinates, check our sunlight numbers against NASA's published illumination maps, and maybe add a page to compare a few sites side by side and export the results.

Overall it's a tool that takes a hard question, "will this spot on the Moon have power and be able to talk to Earth," and lets anyone answer it by clicking around, using real NASA data.
